paper_summary: This paper introduces GRADINO, a configurable, from-scratch data generation framework for producing automatically verifiable numerical QA benchmarks over multiple non-relational tables. GRADINO synthesizes a latent relational source (schema + dense table instantiation) using an LLM, generates executable SQL supervision for multi-table numerical questions (two evidence-flow patterns: parallel and sequential), and renders answer-preserving perturbed non-relational views (hierarchical pivots, merged headers, blank rows, OCR-style noise, unit heterogeneity). Natural-language questions are verbalized from the SQL programs and verified. The authors evaluate state-of-the-art LLMs (gpt-5-mini and several Qwen variants) on financial and environmental scenarios, demonstrating large, domain-dependent performance drops as table count and unit heterogeneity increase. They also show GRADINO data can improve fine-tuned models and report manual verification of generated questions. The paper includes a discussion of limitations, some validation on perturbed real tables, and releases code/data.
summary_of_strengths: 1) Novel and well-motivated problem focus: the paper identifies and operationalizes the important “non-relational multi-table” blind spot in table QA systems — a setting close to real spreadsheets/reports that many benchmarks ignore. 2) Methodological contribution: GRADINO cleanly decouples supervision (latent relational source + SQL) from presentation (non-relational, perturbed views) enabling answer-preserving benchmarking under controlled perturbations (layout, units, noise) and two distinct reasoning topologies (parallel vs sequential). 3) Thorough empirical analysis: experiments across domains, multiple LLMs and table-count regimes convincingly demonstrate sharp scaling failures and the compound effect of unit heterogeneity, including validation on real tables. 4) Practical utility: the generator can both diagnose models and provide training data; combining GRADINO with scarce in-domain data improves performance. 5) Careful design and validation: provenance masks, verifier-based repair of NL questions, manual spot checks, and discussion of limitations and ethical considerations add credibility.
summary_of_weaknesses: 1) Synthetic realism: GRADINO is synthetic by design and, while the paper acknowledges this, more empirical evidence is needed showing that generated perturbations faithfully reflect the distribution and difficulty of naturally occurring non-relational tables across diverse domains. 2) Domain and perturbation scope: experiments are focused on two domains (finance, environmental) and a defined set of perturbations; other important phenomena in real documents (visual alignment cues, chart-table mixtures, more complex tree-shaped joins) are not covered and could change failure modes. 3) Question-verbalization fragility: sequential question verbalization is the most error-prone stage (manual inspection shows ~92.5% correctness), and dropped/altered latent constraints could bias some evaluations; more automated robustness here would strengthen claims. 4) Limited model diversity: evaluation uses gpt-5-mini and Qwen family models. While these are reasonable, results would be more convincing with a broader set of model families (other closed and open LLMs) and ablations of prompting strategies. 5) Evaluation metric sensitivity: normalized EM at 2-decimal precision is reasonable for numeric exactness, but some real-world uses tolerate small numerical tolerance; discussion/experiments on tolerant metrics or error distributions would help interpret practical impact. 6) Comparisons to existing benchmarks: while Table 1 and related discussion position GRADINO relative to prior generation approaches, empirical comparisons (e.g., training on other synthetic datasets) are limited — more direct baselines would clarify the unique value of GRADINO data.
comments_suggestions_typos: Suggestions: (a) Strengthen empirical validation on real-world tables by including additional datasets or a larger perturbed sample from public spreadsheets; (b) add experiments with more LLM families and with/without reasoning prompts (PoT, CoT) to better characterize failure causes; (c) provide more analysis of incorrect predictions (error types: retrieval vs unit-conversion vs arithmetic) to guide mitigation; (d) consider also reporting tolerant numeric metrics (absolute/relative error distributions) in addition to EM; (e) make the released generation configs and prompts easily reusable and document seed/selection details (some prompt text is in the Appendix but central configs should be packaged). Minor: a few places in the main text reference supplementary sections (e.g., §C) — ensure consistent numbering and hyperlinks in final version. Overall the paper is well written with only minor editorial fixes needed.
limitations_and_societal_impact: The authors explicitly discuss several important limitations (synthetic realism, restricted numerical structure, question-verbalization errors, and perturbation coverage) and note privacy considerations (synthetic data; use of public tables for validation). They also discuss that GRADINO is diagnostic and should not be read as a guarantee of real-world performance. This is appropriate. Missing or brief areas: a more in-depth discussion of domain-specific harms (e.g., financial decisions driven by small numeric errors), potential biases introduced by the LLM used to generate schemas/questions, and the extent to which GRADINO covers languages other than English or non-Western numeric conventions (commas for decimals, different calendars) — the latter could matter in cross-lingual or international deployment. Overall the treatment is adequate but could be expanded along these axes.
ethical_concerns: No major ACL-ethics issues. The dataset is synthetic and authors avoid personally identifying information. They use public tables for validation only. The only mild concern is that LLMs are used to generate both training/test artifacts and to produce reasoning traces for fine-tuning; while the authors note potential model bias toward self-generated text, additional explicit analysis of that risk would be useful. The paper documents use of AI assistants for writing and clarifies verification steps.
